originalStudentFacingTitle: Amphipathic lipids self-assemble into bilayers

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: A phospholipid has a polar, water-attracting head and nonpolar hydrocarbon tails that interact poorly with water. Such a molecule is amphipathic: one part is hydrophilic and the other hydrophobic. In an aqueous environment many phospholipids rearrange because exposed tails disrupt favourable interactions among surrounding water molecules.

A bilayer places the heads against the aqueous solutions on both faces and packs the tails inward, away from water. The two layers form a continuous flexible sheet; where a free edge exposes tails, the sheet tends to reseal or curve into an enclosed vesicle. The membrane is a dynamic assembly held together largely by the hydrophobic effect and noncovalent interactions, not by covalent bonds between every lipid.

A synthetic phospholipid vesicle can enclose an aqueous solution even without membrane proteins. This makes a useful model for the lipid foundation of cell boundaries, but a real cell membrane additionally contains diverse proteins and other lipids.

biologyExample: Imagine spilling phospholipids into water: hydrophilic heads remain exposed to water while hydrophobic tails collect inside a sheet or closed vesicle.
essentialTerms: Amphipathic: containing hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions
Bilayer: two opposing leaflets of lipids
Hydrophobic effect: tendency of nonpolar groups to reduce contact with water

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: Phospholipids must be covalently joined into a fixed wall.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Bilayers self-assemble through noncovalent interactions and remain laterally dynamic.

figureRequirements.scientificAltDescription: Conceptual, not-to-scale original illustration for B2.1.1: Amphipathic lipids self-assemble into bilayers. The key principle: Heads face each aqueous environment; both sets of tails face each other in the hydrophobic core.

originalStudentFacingTitle: Hydrophobic cores restrict polar solutes

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: The packed hydrocarbon chains create an energetically unfavourable region for many charged and strongly polar solutes. An ion surrounded by water would have to lose much of its hydration shell to enter this region; large polar molecules also cross extremely slowly.

A lipid bilayer therefore separates the cytosol from an external or organelle solution while still allowing some small uncharged molecules through. This selective barrier is essential: without it cells could not sustain different ion concentrations or create many of the gradients used to do biological work.

A salt solution inside a protein-free vesicle can remain chemically distinct from the surrounding water. The barrier is not perfectly impermeable: permeability depends on molecular properties and time, and biological membranes include transport proteins.

biologyExample: Na+ does not readily cross a protein-free bilayer even if Na+ is more concentrated on one side; its charge and hydration make entry into the core costly.
essentialTerms: Permeability: capacity of a substance to cross a barrier
Hydration shell: oriented water surrounding a solute
Hydrocarbon core: nonpolar membrane interior

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: A bilayer is an absolutely impermeable wall to all molecules.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Permeability varies strongly: small nonpolar molecules cross more easily than ions or large polar solutes.

figureRequirements.scientificAltDescription: Conceptual, not-to-scale original illustration for B2.1.2: Hydrophobic cores restrict polar solutes. The key principle: A charged hydrated ion encounters a nonpolar core; losing its hydration shell is energetically unfavourable.
figureRequirements.rights: Original owner-controlled schematic; rights review pending
figureRequirements.sourceProvenance: Drawn from scratch for Phase 7; no third-party artwork or micrographs imported

activeRecall.answer: A charged hydrated ion encounters a nonpolar core; losing its hydration shell is energetically unfavourable.

originalStudentFacingTitle: Simple diffusion moves small gases down gradients

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: Oxygen and carbon dioxide are small molecules that can dissolve sufficiently in the bilayer interior to pass between phospholipids. They move by random thermal motion; no individual molecule is directed deliberately toward the less concentrated side.

If more molecules are available on one side, statistically more move from that side to the other per unit time than travel back. The result is net diffusion down a concentration gradient. When concentrations become equal, molecules keep moving in both directions, but there is no net flux.

Oxygen diffuses from alveolar air toward oxygen-poor blood cells and across their plasma membranes. Diffusion rate depends on gradient, available surface area, diffusion distance and the permeant molecule's properties.

biologyExample: If dissolved O2 is higher outside a cell, there is net O2 entry although some O2 molecules simultaneously leave.
essentialTerms: Simple diffusion: net passive movement through a bilayer
Concentration gradient: spatial difference in concentration
Dynamic equilibrium: balanced opposing rates

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: At equilibrium all particles stop moving.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Random motion continues; equal opposite fluxes yield zero net diffusion.

figureRequirements.scientificAltDescription: Conceptual, not-to-scale original illustration for B2.1.3: Simple diffusion moves small gases down gradients. The key principle: O2 continues crossing in both directions, with equal average rates so that net flux is zero.
figureRequirements.rights: Original owner-controlled schematic; rights review pending

originalStudentFacingTitle: Integral and peripheral proteins perform distinct roles

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: Proteins in membranes differ in location and form. An integral protein penetrates at least part of the lipid bilayer; many span it fully using hydrophobic amino acid regions that interact with lipid tails. A peripheral protein attaches to one membrane face, often through noncovalent interactions with another protein or polar headgroups.

An integral channel can create a hydrophilic path for selected ions; a membrane receptor can bind an external signalling molecule; and a peripheral protein may help connect the membrane to the cytoskeleton or participate in signalling. Location and molecular shape determine what each protein can do.

In a red blood cell, membrane-spanning transport proteins and peripheral cytoskeletal linkers cooperate to allow exchange while supporting membrane resilience. Not every integral protein is a channel, and not every peripheral protein is outside the cell.

biologyExample: A peripheral protein can be on the cytosolic face; an integral receptor may expose a binding region extracellularly while crossing the hydrocarbon core.
essentialTerms: Integral protein: embedded in a bilayer
Transmembrane protein: spans a bilayer
Peripheral protein: associated with a membrane surface

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: All membrane proteins span the bilayer and transport substances.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Integral and peripheral proteins occupy different positions and perform many non-transport roles.

figureRequirements.scientificAltDescription: Conceptual, not-to-scale original illustration for B2.1.4: Integral and peripheral proteins perform distinct roles. The key principle: Integral is embedded in one or both lipid leaflets; peripheral associates with a membrane face.

originalStudentFacingTitle: Osmosis and aquaporins govern net water movement

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: Water molecules move randomly across a cell membrane, both directly through the lipid bilayer and rapidly through aquaporin channels when present. Osmosis describes a net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane when conditions on either side differ.

In a simplified pair of solutions separated by a membrane permeable to water but not a specified solute, the side with more impermeant dissolved solute has lower water potential and tends to receive net water, all else equal. Water moves both ways; the net flux results from an imbalance in the opposing flows. Hydrostatic pressure and permeant solutes can alter a real system.

An animal cell placed in a solution with a lower effective nonpenetrating solute concentration than its cytosol tends to swell. Aquaporins increase water permeability; they do not 'pump' water against its thermodynamic gradient using ATP.

biologyExample: For a red blood cell in a hypotonic medium, predict swelling, provided relevant solutes cannot rapidly cross the membrane.
essentialTerms: Osmosis: net water movement across selectively permeable boundary
Aquaporin: membrane water channel
Water potential: chemical-potential description of water movement

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: Aquaporins use ATP to actively drive water from dilute to concentrated regions.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Aquaporins are passive water channels; direction of net flux depends on water potential and the solute constraints.

figureRequirements.scientificAltDescription: Conceptual, not-to-scale original illustration for B2.1.5: Osmosis and aquaporins govern net water movement. The key principle: Individual water molecules move randomly; unequal opposing flows produce the net change.

originalStudentFacingTitle: Ion channels enable selective facilitated diffusion

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: An open ion channel forms a hydrated pathway through a membrane's nonpolar interior. The channel's pore geometry and charged or polar residues help favour certain ions over others. Specificity is not simply a matter of an arbitrary hole being large enough.

Ions move through open channels passively down their electrochemical gradients: both the concentration difference and voltage across the membrane can contribute. Opening and closing a channel changes permeability without changing the direction of the ion's driving force by itself.
In neurons, K+ channels can allow K+ to move when their gates are open under a favourable electrochemical gradient. Channel-mediated transport is facilitated diffusion, not energy-coupled pumping.

biologyExample: Predict that closing a Na+-selective channel greatly reduces Na+ permeability even if the sodium gradient remains unchanged.
essentialTerms: Ion channel: selective aqueous pore
Facilitated diffusion: passive transport through protein
Electrochemical gradient: combined electrical and concentration drive

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: A channel drives ions uphill whenever it opens.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Channels allow passive movement down an electrochemical gradient and cannot themselves pump uphill.

figureRequirements.scientificAltDescription: Conceptual, not-to-scale original illustration for B2.1.6: Ion channels enable selective facilitated diffusion. The key principle: It supplies a selective low-energy route; its ions move downhill without the channel consuming ATP to drive transport.

originalStudentFacingTitle: ATP-powered pumps establish concentration gradients

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: To accumulate a solute where it is already abundant, a cell must couple transport to energy. Many pump proteins bind specific particles and change conformation after ATP hydrolysis and associated protein-state changes. The ordered cycle allows transport against a concentration or electrochemical gradient.

The pump must be distinguished from an open pore. A pore would let particles diffuse downhill; a pump undergoes cycles in which access to binding sites alternates between the two sides. Energy supports a direction that would not persist by passive movement alone.
Plant plasma-membrane H+-ATPases use ATP to export protons, building gradients used by other transport processes. Pump specificity means an ATP-powered protein is not a generic conduit for all ions.

biologyExample: A cell sustaining higher proton concentration outside than inside can use an ATP-linked proton pump; opening a proton channel would tend to dissipate this gradient.
essentialTerms: Pump: energy-coupled carrier
ATP hydrolysis: reaction releasing usable chemical free energy
Primary active transport: direct energy coupling

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: ATP is required for all transport mediated by proteins.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Facilitated diffusion uses proteins but is passive; ATP-linked pumps can move particles uphill.

figureRequirements.scientificAltDescription: Conceptual, not-to-scale original illustration for B2.1.7: ATP-powered pumps establish concentration gradients. The key principle: A channel permits downhill transport; a pump couples a conformational cycle to energy to move solutes uphill.

originalStudentFacingTitle: Membranes combine selective and property-dependent permeability

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: Simple diffusion through phospholipids is governed by molecular features, especially size and polarity or charge, rather than recognition by a binding site. Small hydrophobic molecules tend to permeate readily; ions and many large hydrophilic molecules require specialized pathways.

Selective proteins can provide extra routes. A channel permits some ions but not others; a carrier recognizes a substrate and changes shape; a pump can use energy to build gradients. Together, bilayer chemistry and proteins make a membrane selectively permeable.

Two molecules of similar size can cross at very different rates if one is charged and the other nonpolar. Predicting permeability therefore requires identifying the molecular species and which functional transport proteins are present.

biologyExample: A membrane with a glucose carrier may transport glucose significantly faster than an otherwise identical membrane lacking the carrier; this does not mean the bilayer itself has become nonpolar.
essentialTerms: Selective permeability: different crossing rates for different substances
Carrier protein: substrate-binding transporter
Partitioning: distribution between lipid and aqueous phases

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: Simple diffusion selects a substance using specific protein binding sites.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Bilayer permeability depends mainly on physical properties; protein-mediated transport contributes specificity.

originalStudentFacingTitle: Extracellular glycans assist recognition and adhesion

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: Many membrane proteins and lipids carry short or branched carbohydrate chains. A glycoprotein contains a covalently attached carbohydrate on a protein; a glycolipid bears carbohydrate on a lipid. For plasma membranes, these carbohydrate moieties generally project on the extracellular surface.

Surface carbohydrates contribute to molecular recognition and adhesion. Their differing sugar sequences and arrangements can influence which cell-associated proteins or neighbouring cells interact. Specific adhesion often requires specialized binding proteins rather than sugars alone.

The ABO blood-group antigens are carbohydrate structures displayed on red-cell surface molecules, providing a concrete example of recognition. A diagram should not place these glycans projecting from the cytosolic face of the plasma membrane.

biologyExample: ABO antigens illustrate how different external carbohydrate structures can be recognized; they are not identical to membrane transport pores.

Glycolipid: lipid carrying carbohydrate
Glycocalyx: carbohydrate-rich outer surface

originalStudentFacingTitle: The fluid mosaic model integrates lipid and protein components

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: The fluid mosaic model describes proteins embedded in or attached to a laterally mobile lipid bilayer. The hydrophilic phosphate heads contact water, and the nonpolar tails face inward. Integral proteins intersect the lipid matrix; peripheral proteins attach to one face.

An accurate two-dimensional diagram for this understanding should label phospholipids, hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions, an integral protein, a peripheral protein, extracellular carbohydrate on a glycoprotein, and cholesterol positioned among hydrocarbon tails. Not every lipid or protein moves freely: the cytoskeleton and interactions can restrict mobility.
Fluid does not mean membranes dissolve or become random soup. The bilayer remains an organized barrier while components move or reorganize on biologically relevant timescales.

biologyExample: When labelling a model, place a carbohydrate branch on the extracellular side of a membrane-spanning glycoprotein and cholesterol within the tail-rich region.
essentialTerms: Fluid mosaic: dynamic lipid matrix with varied proteins
Cholesterol: sterol in animal membranes
Membrane asymmetry: differences between membrane faces

misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Many components diffuse laterally, but interactions and cellular structures create localized domains.

originalStudentFacingTitle: Fatty-acid saturation tunes membrane flexibility

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: Saturated hydrocarbon tails pack relatively tightly, whereas cis double bonds in unsaturated tails introduce bends that disrupt close packing. Lipids with more unsaturated fatty acids generally have lower melting or phase-transition temperatures than otherwise comparable saturated lipids.

At low temperatures, increasing the proportion of unsaturated chains can help prevent the bilayer becoming excessively ordered and rigid. Saturated chains may help maintain ordered structure at higher temperatures. This adaptation concerns the lipid mixture, not an individual lipid switching between saturated and unsaturated states.

Many cold-adapted organisms adjust fatty-acid composition to sustain membrane function. The exact response depends on organism, lipid type and environmental constraints, so avoid claiming a universal fixed percentage.

biologyExample: Compare two otherwise similar bilayers: the one richer in cis-unsaturated tails usually maintains greater lateral mobility at the same cool temperature.
essentialTerms: Saturated chain: lacks carbon–carbon double bonds
Unsaturated chain: contains double bond(s)
Homeoviscous adaptation: lipid adjustments maintaining useful fluidity

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: Unsaturated chains are straight and therefore pack more tightly.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Cis double bonds cause kinks that generally reduce packing and transition temperature.

originalStudentFacingTitle: Cholesterol buffers animal membrane fluidity

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: Cholesterol is an amphipathic sterol with a small polar hydroxyl group near phospholipid heads and a largely hydrophobic ring system inserted among fatty-acid tails. Its position matters: it is not a free aqueous solute or a pore.

At relatively high temperatures cholesterol can constrain lipid movement and reduce excessive permeability; at low temperatures it interrupts close packing and helps resist abrupt rigidification. Its net influence depends on temperature and lipid composition, so saying it simply increases fluidity in every context is wrong.

Animal plasma membranes often contain cholesterol as a fluidity modulator. The functional consequence is stability of membrane behaviour across varying conditions rather than turning the membrane into a solid sheet.

biologyExample: Predict why a cholesterol-rich bilayer may show a less sharp transition between ordered and disordered phases compared with the corresponding cholesterol-free mixture.
essentialTerms: Sterol: lipid with a fused-ring framework
Fluidity buffer: component moderating changes in membrane order
Phase transition: change in lipid organization

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: Cholesterol always increases membrane fluidity, regardless of temperature.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: It can restrain movement at high temperature and impede tight packing at low temperature.

originalStudentFacingTitle: Membrane flexibility permits endocytosis and exocytosis

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: Membrane lipids can curve and reorganize, allowing small membrane-bound compartments to form and fuse. In endocytosis the plasma membrane invaginates, encloses material and pinches off into the cell. The material becomes separated from the cytosol by a vesicle membrane.

In exocytosis an intracellular vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane, releasing its lumenal contents to the exterior. The two processes move material by changing membrane topology rather than by pushing whole proteins through lipid tails. Cellular machinery and energy-dependent steps may be involved in actual vesicle traffic.

Receptor-mediated uptake of low-density lipoprotein particles exemplifies endocytosis; secretion of a peptide hormone exemplifies exocytosis. Fluidity makes membrane bending and fusion physically possible, but it is not sufficient alone to specify cargo or trigger fusion.

biologyExample: A cell secreting a protein releases its vesicle lumen to the extracellular environment when vesicle and plasma membranes fuse.
essentialTerms: Endocytosis: uptake by inward membrane budding
Exocytosis: secretion by membrane fusion
Vesicle: small membrane-enclosed compartment

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: Exocytosis is a protein molecule diffusing between phospholipids.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Exocytosis involves fusion of a vesicle membrane with the plasma membrane and transfer of vesicular cargo.

originalStudentFacingTitle: Chemical and voltage signals gate neuronal channels

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: A gated ion channel switches accessibility in response to a defined signal. At a neuromuscular junction, nicotinic acetylcholine receptors bind acetylcholine on the extracellular side. Their opening permits cation flux, producing a depolarizing response in the muscle end plate under physiological conditions.

Voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels instead respond to changes in membrane potential. Their distinct activation and inactivation kinetics help shape an action potential: rapid Na+ permeability changes usually contribute to depolarization, while delayed K+ permeability contributes to repolarization.

Gating changes whether ions have a pathway; an open channel still permits movement only down the relevant electrochemical gradient. A neurotransmitter-gated receptor is not the same mechanism as a voltage sensor even if both can contribute to electrical signalling.

biologyExample: Acetylcholine binding opens its receptor channel; a later voltage change can activate voltage-gated Na+ channels in an excitable membrane.
essentialTerms: Ligand-gated channel: gated by molecular binding
Voltage-gated channel: gated by membrane voltage
Depolarization: reduction in inside-negative membrane potential

originalStudentFacingTitle: The sodium–potassium pump exchanges ions and maintains gradients

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: The animal Na+/K+-ATPase is an integral membrane exchange transporter that cycles through ion-binding conformations. For each ATP hydrolyzed, its typical physiological cycle exports three Na+ ions from the cytosol and imports two K+ ions. Both transport directions oppose prevailing electrochemical gradients.

This electrogenic exchange moves one net positive charge outward per cycle. It contributes directly to membrane potential and, crucially, maintains the Na+ and K+ gradients that channels exploit. Most immediate resting membrane potential is associated with permeability, notably to K+, so do not imply the pump alone creates the full resting potential.

During repeated nerve activity, gradients would gradually dissipate without pump action. The ATPase supports future excitability even though the rapid upstroke of an action potential results primarily from opening channels, not from a burst of pump cycles.

biologyExample: With pump operation, intracellular K+ remains relatively high and intracellular Na+ relatively low, sustaining potential energy for downstream transport.
essentialTerms: Na+/K+-ATPase: ATP-linked exchange pump
Electrogenic: transfers net electrical charge
Resting potential: membrane voltage in the unstimulated state

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: The pump moves three K+ out and two Na+ in, directly producing every action potential.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: It moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP, maintaining gradients; action potentials rely on gated channels.

originalStudentFacingTitle: Sodium gradients power glucose cotransport

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: A sodium-dependent glucose cotransporter binds Na+ and glucose on the same side of a membrane and alternates access to deliver both inward. The favourable electrochemical entry of Na+ supplies energy that can drive glucose uptake against its glucose concentration gradient. This is secondary or indirect active transport.

The Na+ gradient is maintained chiefly by basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase using ATP. Therefore the cotransporter does not hydrolyze ATP directly in its transport step, but the overall process ultimately depends on ATP-powered gradient maintenance. Glucose can then leave the enterocyte across its basolateral membrane using an appropriate facilitated transporter when its gradient allows.

This arrangement enables glucose absorption by small-intestinal epithelial cells and reabsorption in proximal nephron tubules. Different SGLT isoforms differ in coupling ratio; do not label all sodium–glucose cotransporters with a single universal stoichiometry.

biologyExample: If the basolateral Na+/K+ pump is persistently inhibited, the Na+ gradient weakens and Na+-linked glucose uptake at the apical surface will become less effective.
essentialTerms: Symport: two substances transported in the same direction
Secondary active transport: uphill flux coupled to downhill solute flux
Enterocyte: small-intestinal absorptive epithelial cell

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: A sodium–glucose cotransporter obtains ATP directly every time it imports glucose.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: It couples glucose import to downhill Na+ entry; ATP use is indirect through gradient-generating pumps.

figureRequirements.scientificAltDescription: Conceptual, not-to-scale original illustration for B2.1.16: Sodium gradients power glucose cotransport. The key principle: ATPase lowers intracellular Na+; Na+ subsequently moves downhill through an apical SGLT and can drive glucose uptake uphill.

originalStudentFacingTitle: Cell-adhesion molecules hold tissues together

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: Cell-adhesion molecules (CAMs) are cell-surface proteins that help cells attach to adjacent cells or relevant extracellular structures. By providing selective molecular recognition and physical links, CAMs help organize cells into tissues and maintain structural integrity.

Different intercellular junction types employ different adhesion proteins; the IB understanding requires this principle rather than a memorized catalogue of every protein or junction. CAM-mediated binding is not identical to fusion of adjacent plasma membranes. Adhesion often works with intracellular cytoskeletal linkages and tissue mechanics.

In epithelial tissue, cell-cell adhesion helps neighbouring cells remain connected as a continuous layer despite mechanical stresses. Defective adhesion can compromise tissue cohesion even while each individual cell's lipid bilayer remains intact.

biologyExample: Predict that weakening cell–cell adhesion proteins could disrupt an epithelium without having to dissolve all its cell membranes.
essentialTerms: Cell-adhesion molecule: molecule mediating physical cell attachment
Cell junction: specialized connection between cells
Tissue: organized group of interacting cells

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: Cells in a tissue share one continuous fused plasma membrane.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Neighbouring cells retain distinct membranes and are attached by cell-adhesion systems and junctions.

figureRequirements.scientificAltDescription: Conceptual, not-to-scale original illustration for B2.1.17: Cell-adhesion molecules hold tissues together. The key principle: Different junctions use different adhesion molecules to make and stabilize specific cell-cell contacts.

originalStudentFacingTitle: Organelles are cell subunits specialized for functions

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: A cell is not simply an unorganized bag of molecules. An organelle is a distinct cell subunit with a specific function; in this course the nucleus, ribosomes, vesicles and plasma membrane count as organelles. A cell wall, cytoskeleton and cytoplasm are important structures but are not classified as organelles by this IB syllabus.

Organelle identity is determined by its structures and activities rather than whether it is enclosed by one membrane. Ribosomes are non-membrane-bound particles with a key role in protein synthesis. The nucleus encloses genetic material; vesicles store or transport cargo; the plasma membrane provides the selective boundary between cell interior and exterior.

Scientists learned organelle functions by fractionating homogenized cells using differences in size and density, then testing isolated fractions for characteristic enzymes or activities. The ultracentrifuge and improved cell-fractionation procedures were major technique advances, but fraction purity and contamination must be considered before identifying where a reaction takes place.

biologyExample: A fraction rich in mitochondria is expected to exhibit markers of aerobic ATP-production machinery, provided fraction purity is checked against contaminating organelles.
essentialTerms: Organelle: discrete, functionally specialized cell subunit
Cell fractionation: separating cell components after disruption
Ultracentrifugation: high-speed separation according to physical properties

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: Only membrane-bounded particles can ever count as organelles in this course.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Ribosomes are organelles under the IB wording even though they are not enclosed by a lipid membrane.

figureRequirements.scientificAltDescription: Original conceptual cell-biology illustration for B2.2.1, not to scale: Organelles are cell subunits specialized for functions. Recall explanation: Nuclei, vesicles, ribosomes and plasma membranes count; cell wall, cytoskeleton and cytoplasm do not.

originalStudentFacingTitle: Separating transcription and translation permits RNA processing

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: In a eukaryotic cell, transcription produces an RNA transcript from DNA inside the nucleus. Translation occurs at ribosomes in the cytoplasm. The nuclear envelope separates these activities spatially so that the transcript can be modified and checked before it encounters cytoplasmic ribosomes.

Many eukaryotic protein-coding transcripts undergo processing, such as intron removal by splicing and terminal modifications, before mature mRNA exits through a nuclear pore. This separation allows regulated production and export of mRNA; not all RNA is processed identically, and some organelles also contain their own translation systems.

Most prokaryotes lack a membrane-enclosed nucleus, so ribosomes can begin translating an mRNA while it is still being transcribed. This difference illustrates why compartment structure changes the timing and control of gene expression.

biologyExample: A freshly transcribed nuclear pre-mRNA can have introns removed before the mature mRNA exits to the cytosolic ribosome.
essentialTerms: Transcription: RNA synthesis from DNA template
Translation: protein synthesis by ribosomes
Splicing: removal of introns from RNA transcript

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: Translation of nuclear genes normally takes place inside the nucleus.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: For nuclear-encoded cytosolic/secretory proteins, translation occurs at ribosomes in the cytoplasm after RNA export.

figureRequirements.scientificAltDescription: Original conceptual cell-biology illustration for B2.2.2, not to scale: Separating transcription and translation permits RNA processing. Recall explanation: RNA can be processed and regulated in the nucleus before mature mRNA encounters cytoplasmic ribosomes.

figureRequirements.sourceProvenance: New diagram authored for Phase 7, with no imported micrographs or commercial imagery

activeRecall.question: State the temporal advantage of separating nucleus from cytoplasm.
activeRecall.answer: RNA can be processed and regulated in the nucleus before mature mRNA encounters cytoplasmic ribosomes.

originalStudentFacingTitle: Cytoplasmic compartments concentrate and isolate reactions

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: Membrane boundaries can concentrate particular enzymes and substrates inside a small space, so reactants encounter the correct catalysts without being diluted throughout the cytosol. Compartment membranes also establish controlled pH or ion composition, supporting distinct biochemical environments.

Some pathways would interfere with other processes if all their enzymes and products were released into one common aqueous pool. Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes that operate effectively in an acidic lumen, while the surrounding cytosol normally has a different environment. A phagocytic vacuole can enclose ingested material and fuse with lysosomes so digestion occurs in a bounded space.

Compartmentalization does not imply total isolation: transporters and vesicular traffic selectively move substances between compartments. Its benefit lies in combining separation with controlled exchange, not sealing each reaction off permanently.

biologyExample: After a macrophage engulfs a microbe into a phagosome, fusion with lysosomes delivers digestive enzymes to the internal compartment instead of releasing them throughout cytosol.
essentialTerms: Lysosome: acidic organelle containing hydrolytic enzymes
Phagosome: phagocytically formed membrane-bound vacuole
Compartmentalization: segregation into specialized cell spaces

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: Every biochemical process improves if enzymes and substrates are freely mixed in cytosol.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Enrichment, pH specialization and separation of potentially conflicting reactions can require membrane-bound compartments.

figureRequirements.scientificAltDescription: Original conceptual cell-biology illustration for B2.2.3, not to scale: Cytoplasmic compartments concentrate and isolate reactions. Recall explanation: Enzyme/metabolite concentration and incompatible-reaction separation; lysosomes and phagocytic vacuoles illustrate bounded digestion.

figureRequirements.sourceProvenance: New diagram authored for Phase 7, with no imported micrographs or commercial imagery

originalStudentFacingTitle: Mitochondrial architecture supports aerobic ATP synthesis

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: Mitochondria have an outer membrane and an extensively folded inner membrane. Electron-transport complexes and ATP synthase are associated with the inner membrane. Its cristae increase surface area for this membrane-based energy conversion without proportionately increasing organelle volume.

Respiratory electron transport helps move protons from matrix toward the small intermembrane space. The resulting electrochemical difference across the inner membrane can drive ATP production when protons return through ATP synthase. A relatively small intermembrane compartment helps support a steep change in proton concentration under suitable conditions.

The matrix contains enzymes and substrates for reactions including the Krebs cycle. Keeping these reactions in the matrix and oxidative phosphorylation machinery in the inner membrane makes the pathway organized and coupled. ATP synthesis is not explained merely by folds increasing 'space for oxygen'.

biologyExample: A mitochondrion with extensively developed cristae provides more inner-membrane area for the protein complexes used in oxidative phosphorylation.
essentialTerms: Crista: inward fold of mitochondrial inner membrane
Matrix: mitochondrial innermost compartment
Proton-motive force: proton electrochemical gradient across a membrane

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: The Krebs cycle runs on the cristae because every respiration enzyme is membrane-bound.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Krebs-cycle enzymes/substrates are primarily in the matrix, while electron-transport machinery is associated with the inner membrane.

figureRequirements.scientificAltDescription: Original conceptual cell-biology illustration for B2.2.4, not to scale: Mitochondrial architecture supports aerobic ATP synthesis. Recall explanation: Cristae: inner-membrane area; small intermembrane space: gradient compartment; matrix: Krebs enzymes/substrates; double membrane: distinct spaces.

figureRequirements.sourceProvenance: New diagram authored for Phase 7, with no imported micrographs or commercial imagery

originalStudentFacingTitle: Chloroplast membrane spaces organize photosynthesis

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: A chloroplast has an outer and inner envelope and a further internal system of thylakoid membranes. Photosystems and associated electron-transfer components occupy the thylakoid membranes, providing a large area where light energy can drive electron transport.

During the light-dependent reactions, protons can accumulate in the small thylakoid lumen, helping establish the electrochemical gradient that powers ATP synthase. The geometry of many thylakoid membranes and a small enclosed fluid space supports efficient coupling of light capture to energy conversion.

The stroma surrounds the thylakoids and contains enzymes and substrates for the Calvin cycle. This separation links light-dependent production of ATP and reducing power to enzymatic carbon fixation without pretending that the thylakoid lumen and the stroma are the same compartment.

biologyExample: An actively photosynthesizing chloroplast uses thylakoid photosystems to capture light energy while Calvin-cycle enzymes operate in stroma.
essentialTerms: Thylakoid: flattened membrane-bounded chloroplast sac
Lumen: inner fluid space of thylakoid
Stroma: chloroplast fluid outside thylakoids

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: Chloroplast photosystems are in the stroma and the Calvin cycle occurs inside thylakoid lumens.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Photosystems are embedded in thylakoid membranes; Calvin-cycle enzymes operate in the stroma.

figureRequirements.scientificAltDescription: Original conceptual cell-biology illustration for B2.2.5, not to scale: Chloroplast membrane spaces organize photosynthesis. Recall explanation: Thylakoid membrane, thylakoid lumen and stroma, respectively.

originalStudentFacingTitle: A double nuclear envelope regulates exchange and division

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: The nuclear envelope comprises an inner and outer membrane separated by a perinuclear space. The double-membrane boundary helps maintain a distinct nucleoplasmic environment containing chromosomes and RNA-processing machinery. The outer nuclear membrane is continuous with endoplasmic reticulum.

Nuclear pore complexes span both membranes and regulate traffic such as import of nuclear proteins and export of RNA-protein assemblies. A nucleus without pores would fail to exchange materials required for gene expression and DNA maintenance. Pores are selective gates, not accidental rips.

In many eukaryotic cells undergoing open mitosis and meiosis, the nuclear envelope disassembles, with membrane components dispersing into ER-associated structures and vesicular material, then reassembles around separated chromosomes. This temporally reorganizes nuclear access for chromosome segregation; closed mitosis in some organisms is an important wider biological exception.

biologyExample: An mRNA ready for cytoplasmic translation must pass through a nuclear pore; a large protein needing to reach the nucleus may require a nuclear-localization signal.
essentialTerms: Nuclear envelope: double membrane surrounding nucleus
Nuclear pore complex: selective transport channel
Open mitosis: division with envelope disassembly

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: The nuclear envelope has no pores and must always dissolve whenever an RNA leaves.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Pore complexes permit regulated nucleocytoplasmic traffic during interphase; envelope breakdown is associated with nuclear division.

figureRequirements.scientificAltDescription: Original conceptual cell-biology illustration for B2.2.6, not to scale: A double nuclear envelope regulates exchange and division. Recall explanation: Segregates nuclear processing, permits selective pore traffic; in open mitosis/meiosis, envelope disassembles and later reforms.

figureRequirements.sourceProvenance: New diagram authored for Phase 7, with no imported micrographs or commercial imagery

originalStudentFacingTitle: Free and ER-bound ribosomes serve different protein destinations

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: All ribosomes translate mRNA into polypeptides. Free ribosomes in the cytosol commonly synthesize proteins that remain and function in cytosol or are directed to certain non-secretory compartments after synthesis. This explains their prevalence where intracellular metabolic enzymes are produced.

Ribosomes bound to rough endoplasmic reticulum synthesize many proteins destined for secretion, the endomembrane system or insertion into membranes. A nascent signal sequence can recruit the ribosome to the ER, where the polypeptide is threaded into or across its membrane as synthesis continues. The ribosome itself is not permanently of one type; a given ribosome can participate in free or membrane-bound translation at different times.

The rough appearance under microscopy comes from ribosomes decorating the cytosolic surface of the ER. For instance, a secreted digestive enzyme typically enters the ER pathway, whereas a cytosolic glycolysis enzyme commonly emerges on a free ribosome.

biologyExample: Predict that a polypeptide with a suitable ER targeting sequence is synthesized into the ER pathway even though ribosomes are structurally of the same basic type.
essentialTerms: Rough ER: ER membrane with attached ribosomes
Signal sequence: targeting information in a nascent protein
Co-translational translocation: entry into ER during synthesis

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: Rough ER produces all proteins while free ribosomes make only RNA.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Both synthesize proteins; protein targeting controls whether translation becomes ER-associated or stays free in cytosol.

figureRequirements.scientificAltDescription: Original conceptual cell-biology illustration for B2.2.7, not to scale: Free and ER-bound ribosomes serve different protein destinations. Recall explanation: Free: cytosolic enzymes; bound: proteins entering secretory or endomembrane pathway.

originalStudentFacingTitle: Golgi cisternae process and dispatch secretory proteins

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: The Golgi apparatus consists of a polarized stack of membrane-bounded cisternae with associated vesicular carriers. Proteins arriving from the ER travel through Golgi-associated compartments where many are modified, sorted and packaged for subsequent transport.

Protein processing may include further glycan modification or proteolytic maturation, depending on the product. Different destinations require sorting information and transport machinery: a secretory protein headed outside the cell is not handled exactly like a protein intended for a lysosome.

In a cell secreting peptide hormones, a secretory cargo typically enters rough ER, passes through Golgi processing, and is packed into vesicles that later fuse with the plasma membrane. The Golgi does not transcribe genes or act as the primary site of translation.

biologyExample: Trace a secreted protein: ribosome on rough ER → ER lumen → transport carriers → Golgi cisternae → secretory vesicle → cell surface.
essentialTerms: Golgi cisterna: flattened membrane-bounded compartment
Protein sorting: routing of cargo to destinations
Secretory vesicle: cargo-containing membrane compartment

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: Proteins are translated by Golgi ribosomes, then transported to rough ER for processing.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Translation of secretory proteins occurs on rough ER; Golgi acts later in processing, sorting and secretion.

figureRequirements.scientificAltDescription: Original conceptual cell-biology illustration for B2.2.8, not to scale: Golgi cisternae process and dispatch secretory proteins. Recall explanation: Rough ER synthesis → vesicular delivery → Golgi processing/sorting → secretory vesicle → plasma membrane fusion.

originalStudentFacingTitle: Clathrin-coated vesicles help sort membrane cargo

textbookReference.bibliography: Clegg, Davis and Talbot, Biology for the IB Diploma Programme, 3rd ed., Hodder Education (2023)

explanationRequirements.originalAuthoredText: Vesicles are membrane-enclosed compartments that move selected material within cells and between the cell interior and plasma membrane. In a canonical clathrin-mediated endocytic pathway, cargo receptors recruit adaptor proteins on the cytosolic membrane face, which in turn recruit clathrin into a curved coat.

Clathrin forms a lattice supporting pit curvature; additional proteins assist membrane constriction and scission. After budding, the coat is removed before downstream fusion and sorting. Clathrin is outside the budding vesicle membrane, not a soluble component floating within its lumen.

Cells use vesicles to traffic membrane receptors and other cargo, preserving distinctions between the cytosol and vesicle lumen. Not every vesicle uses clathrin: other coat systems also operate in cells. The syllabus specifically requires understanding clathrin's role in forming some vesicles.

biologyExample: A coated pit concentrating surface receptors buds inward; its clathrin coat faces cytosol and is typically disassembled before the new vesicle fuses with an endosome.
essentialTerms: Clathrin: coat protein supporting coated-pit formation
Adaptor: link between cargo receptors and coat
Uncoating: coat removal after vesicle budding

misconceptionAndCorrection.misconception: Clathrin is packed as cargo inside every vesicle and remains there after fusion.
misconceptionAndCorrection.correction: Clathrin coats the cytosolic surface of selected budding vesicles and commonly dissociates after budding.

figureRequirements.scientificAltDescription: Original conceptual cell-biology illustration for B2.2.9, not to scale: Clathrin-coated vesicles help sort membrane cargo. Recall explanation: On the cytosolic surface as a coat assembled through adaptors; it is not the lumenal cargo.
figureRequirements.rights: Original owner-controlled schematic; rights review pending
figureRequirements.sourceProvenance: New diagram authored for Phase 7, with no imported micrographs or commercial imagery
